Series::bernoulli¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::bernoulli() const
Series Series::bernoulli(double p) const

What It Does¶

Returns a new Series of independent 0/1 outcomes — one coin flip per element — without touching the receiver. (The in-place counterpart is bernoulli_.)

The two overloads answer different questions:

  • bernoulli() — every receiver element is its own success probability. The receiver must be floating-point and every value must be finite and in [0, 1]; invalid probabilities are rejected, not clipped. Use this when a probability model has already produced a Series.

  • bernoulli(p) — the receiver values are ignored; it contributes only the output shape, dtype, and platform, and every position uses the same p. Use this when an existing Series is just the shape you want. This overload (like bernoulli_) also accepts integer and Bool receivers — only complex is rejected.

The result keeps the receiver’s dtype — it is not a Bool mask (unless the receiver was already Bool).

Reproducibility¶

Deterministic given the process-wide RNG seed. Call pluss::rng_seed(seed) before sampling to fix the outcomes; two runs from the same seed produce equal tensors. Each call advances a stream counter.

Parameters¶

p (double, for the one-argument form): the shared success probability. Must be finite and in [0, 1]. p = 0 fills with zeros, p = 1 with ones.

Returns¶

Series A new tensor of 0/1 outcomes with the receiver’s shape, dtype, and platform. The receiver is unchanged.

Raises¶

  • bernoulli(): if the receiver is not floating-point, or any element is non-finite or outside [0, 1]

  • bernoulli(p): if the receiver dtype is complex, or p is non-finite or outside [0, 1]

Gradient¶

Not differentiable — the outcomes carry no derivative back to the probabilities.

Examples¶

Example 1. bernoulli() — the receiver values are the per-element probabilities.

auto p = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, p.bernoulli());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 1.0000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

Probability 0 can never succeed and probability 1 can never fail, so this draw is deterministic.

Example 2. bernoulli(p) ignores the receiver values — it uses only the shape and dtype.

pluss::rng_seed(42);
auto canvas = pluss::series::zeros({10}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
auto out = canvas.bernoulli(0.5);
std::cout << "canvas unchanged: "; pluss::series::print(std::cout, canvas);
std::cout << "out = "; pluss::series::print(std::cout, out);

Output¶

canvas unchanged: Series(shape=[10], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=10, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000]out = Series(shape=[10], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=10, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

The ten 0.0s in canvas did not force failures — this overload uses 0.5, not the receiver’s values — and canvas itself is untouched.

Example 3. bernoulli() diagnoses out-of-range probabilities before producing anything.

try {
  pluss::make_series({-0.1, 0.5}).bernoulli();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string m = e.what();
  std::cout << m.substr(0, m.find('\n')) << "\n";
}
try {
  pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.2}).bernoulli();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string m = e.what();
  std::cout << m.substr(0, m.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

bernoulli: probabilities must be finite and in [0, 1]
bernoulli: probabilities must be finite and in [0, 1]

Example 4. Reproducible under a fixed seed; the receiver is never modified.

pluss::rng_seed(3);
auto p = pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5});
auto a = p.bernoulli();
pluss::rng_seed(3);
auto b = p.bernoulli();
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "a == b: " << a.equal(b) << "  p unchanged: ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, p);

Output¶

a == b: true  p unchanged: Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5000, 0.5000, 0.5000, 0.5000]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • bernoulli() reads the receiver as probabilities; bernoulli(p) ignores them. Pick the overload deliberately.

  • bernoulli() requires a floating-point receiver with every value in [0, 1]; NaN, infinity, and out-of-range values fail up front — they are not clipped.

  • The result keeps the receiver dtype — it is not a Bool mask.

  • Use bernoulli_ instead only when overwriting the receiver is the intent.

  • Reproducible only after pluss::rng_seed(seed); each call advances the stream.

  • Not differentiable.

Summary¶

bernoulli() / bernoulli(p) returns a new 0/1 tensor:

  • bernoulli() uses each receiver element as its own probability (floating-point, values in [0, 1])

  • bernoulli(p) ignores receiver values, uses shared p, accepts integer / Bool / floating receivers

  • receiver is never modified; result keeps its dtype

  • reproducible under pluss::rng_seed(seed); not differentiable

See Also¶

  • Series::bernoulli_: the in-place form — fills the receiver instead of returning a new tensor.

  • Series::multinomial: draw category indices from nonnegative weights.

  • Series::random_: uniform integers over a range.
